pattern: Accept fast, deliver asynchronously: validate and persist the request, enforce policy (preferences, caps) at one gate, then route into per-class queues drained by workers that own retries, idempotency and the rate limits of slow, unreliable third parties.

tips.nudge: How many different ways can you reach a user here?
tips.hint: List the channels the platform must support.
tips.show: F1: Send notifications by mobile push (iOS/Android), SMS and email.

checks.label: Who asks for notifications, and how

tips.nudge: The users of this platform are not end users. Who are they?
tips.hint: Describe how internal services and campaigns request a send (now or scheduled).
tips.show: F2: Internal services send a notification (to one user, or scheduled to a segment for campaigns) using a template and parameters.

checks.label: Recipient control over what they receive

tips.nudge: A user turned off marketing email last week. What must happen?
tips.hint: Capture per-category / per-channel opt-outs and the frequency cap.
tips.show: F3: Users opt out per category and channel; marketing is capped at N per user per day; suppressed sends are recorded.

tips.nudge: A login code silently disappears. Or arrives three times. Which is worse, and what do you promise?
tips.hint: State what happens to an accepted request and how duplicates are treated.
tips.show: N1: Accepted notifications are never lost (at-least-once to the provider) and duplicates are suppressed by idempotency key.

checks.label: Not all messages are equally urgent

tips.nudge: Login code vs. weekend sale: same latency expectation?
tips.hint: Give each class its own latency target.
tips.show: N2: Transactional (OTP, resets) delivered to the provider within ~5 s p99 even during campaigns; marketing may lag minutes.

tips.nudge: 500M a day is how many per second? And during a campaign?
tips.hint: daily total ÷ seconds per day, then × the burst factor.
tips.show: 500M/day ≈ 5.8k /s average; campaign bursts ×10 ≈ 58k /s.

tips.nudge: Each notification leaves a record. How many, how big, for how long?
tips.hint: per day × retention days × bytes per record.

checks.label: Size of the contact/device data estimated

tips.nudge: How much space do 300M device tokens take? Could it all sit in a cache?
tips.hint: devices × bytes per row (token ~ 100–200 B plus ids and metadata).
tips.show: 300M × ~250 B ≈ 75 GB: fits in a modest cache cluster.

tips.nudge: What does the orders team call when an order ships?
tips.hint: A POST with recipient, template, parameters, category and an idempotency key; respond before delivery happens.
tips.show: POST /notifications {user_id, template, params, category, channels?, idempotency_key, send_at?} → 202 {notification_id}

tips.nudge: How does the app register a phone or record an opt-out?
tips.hint: Endpoints for device registration and preference updates.
tips.show: PUT /users/{id}/preferences {category, channel, enabled}; POST /users/{id}/devices {platform, push_token}

checks.label: Where to reach a user modelled

tips.nudge: Push needs something per phone that Apple/Google gave you.
tips.hint: Model each user's devices and addresses.
tips.show: devices(user_id, device_id, platform, push_token, updated_at); contacts(user_id, email, phone).

tips.nudge: Teams ask 'did my notification go out?'. Where's the answer?
tips.hint: Record each notification and its state transitions.
tips.show: notification_log(notification_id, idempotency_key, user_id, channel, status: queued|sent|failed|suppressed, attempts, provider_id, ts) TTL 30d.

tips.nudge: Where does the platform look up opt-outs on every send?
tips.hint: A preferences store, fronted by a cache for the hot path.
tips.show: Preferences + devices in SQL, read through a cache by the notification API.

tips.nudge: Apple takes 2 s to answer. Should the orders service wait?
tips.hint: Accept, persist, and put work somewhere durable for later processing.
tips.show: Notification API → per-channel queues → channel workers.

checks.label: Hand-off to the outside world drawn

tips.nudge: Who actually delivers to the phone or inbox?
tips.hint: Show which component talks to each third-party provider.
tips.show: Push workers → APNs/FCM, SMS workers → SMS vendor, email workers → email vendor.

tips.nudge: The SMS vendor times out after you sent the request. Did the SMS go out?
tips.hint: Decide retry policy and how you avoid duplicates on retry.
tips.show: Retry with exponential backoff + jitter via a delay queue, then a dead-letter queue; idempotency key per (notification, channel) sent to the provider and checked in the log.

checks.label: How different message types share capacity

tips.nudge: A 50M-message campaign is queued. A login code arrives behind it. Then what?
tips.hint: Think about separating traffic by urgency and by channel.
tips.show: Separate queues (and worker pools) per channel × priority: transactional never waits behind marketing; a slow SMS vendor never blocks push.

checks.label: Volume limits for users and providers decided

tips.nudge: Providers throttle you, and users hate spam. Where do you count?
tips.hint: Decide per-user caps and per-provider send rates, and where they're enforced.
tips.show: Per-user marketing cap checked in the API (counter in Redis); per-provider token buckets in workers so bursts are smoothed instead of rejected.

tips.nudge: The push provider is down for 20 minutes. Walk through what happens.
tips.hint: Cover provider outage, worker crash mid-send and queue backlog.
tips.show: Provider down: messages stay queued, retries back off, circuit breaker stops hammering; worker crash: message not acked, redelivered, idempotency key prevents duplicate; expired OTPs dropped after TTL.

tips.nudge: How would you notice that login codes are slow before users complain?
tips.hint: Metrics per channel and priority, end to end.
tips.show: Queue depth and age per channel×priority, accept→sent latency, provider error/throttle rates, DLQ size, suppression rate, SMS spend.
